title: ProtocolBench: Which LLM MultiAgent Protocol to Choose?
claim: Many competing options exist and choosing among them is unclear; a benchmark measures them and a learned router selects the best.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed dividers, arrow from benchmark into router
description: A wide three-part figure separated by dashed vertical lines. The left part shows the problem. Company logos (Google, Oxford, and others) point with brown arrows to orange protocol boxes labeled A2A, Agora and ACP. Further orange boxes read ANP, MCP, LMOS and 'And more...'. A robot icon with a question mark sits beside the text 'How to choose protocols?'. The middle part is titled ProtocolBench and has a document icon. It stacks four rows. Each row pairs a purple category label (Routing, Safety, Load balance, Recovery) with a pink arrow-shaped scenario (Gaia Document QA, Safety Tech, Streaming Queue, Fail-Storm). The right part is titled ProtocolRouter and has a green circular icon. A brain-circuit graphic sits in the center, with green arrows pointing out to green protocol boxes (ANP, A2A, Agora, ACP). A purple curved arrow runs from the benchmark into the router.
caption: Overview of ProtocolBench and ProtocolRouter. To understand the tradeoff across existing LLM multi-agent protocols, we first design ProtocolBench that covers four core evaluation dimensions, then propose ProtocolRouter to help users select the optimal protocol.
abstract: As large-scale multi-agent systems evolve, the communication protocol layer has become a critical yet under-evaluated factor shaping performance and reliability. Despite the existence of diverse protocols (A2A, ACP, ANP, Agora, etc.), selection is often intuition-driven and lacks standardized guidance. We introduce ProtocolBench, a benchmark that systematically compares agent protocols along four measurable axes: task success, end-to-end latency, message or byte overhead, and robustness under failures. On ProtocolBench, protocol choice significantly influences system behavior. In the Streaming Queue scenario, overall completion time varies by up to 36.5% across protocols, and mean end-to-end latency differs by 3.48 s. Under Fail-Storm Recovery, resilience also differs consistently across protocols. Beyond evaluation, we present ProtocolRouter, a learnable protocol router that selects per-scenario (or per-module) protocols from requirement and runtime signals. ProtocolRouter reduces Fail-Storm recovery time by up to 18.1% versus the best single-protocol baseline, and achieves scenario-specific gains such as higher success in GAIA. We also release ProtocolRouterBench to standardize protocol evaluation and improve reliability at scale.
